findingStatement: Random Forest and XGBoost accuracy decreases near the coastline, and distance from the coastline could be considered as an additional model feature.
findingOutcome: Reduced accuracy near coastlines and a proposed additional coastline-distance feature.

findingStatement: When surface wind observations deviate because of adjacent vegetation and buildings, the transfer model has difficulty obtaining accurate 100 m wind-speed simulations at site level.
findingOutcome: Accurate site-level simulation becomes difficult.

findingStatement: The superiority of PSO-LSTM does not apply uniformly to MBE; FFNN achieved the least MBE at 60 and 80 m, while PSO-LSTM performed better at the remaining heights.
findingOutcome: FFNN had the least MBE at 60 and 80 m; PSO-LSTM performed better at the remaining heights.

findingStatement: As extrapolation height increased, estimated values from all methods deviated more from measurements and performance deteriorated.
findingScope: extrapolation from 50 to 120 m using measured wind speeds at 10–40 m
findingOutcome: Error increased and coefficient-of-determination performance deteriorated with increasing height.

findingStatement: Applying the Weibull distribution to Coxim is not recommended because the station is characterized by low monthly average wind speeds.
findingOutcome: not recommended

findingStatement: Applying the Weibull distribution to Miranda is not recommended because the station is characterized by low monthly average wind speeds.
findingOutcome: not recommended

findingStatement: At Coxim, the graphical method was the best estimator from September to February, although the accuracy of all six methods decreased at this low-wind-speed station.
findingOutcome: graphical method was the best estimator for the specified months

findingStatement: For the three selected sites, EPFM had the best RMSE and R2 performance.
findingOutcome: best performance among the assessed estimation methods

findingStatement: WVM and MoroM were not suitable for determining Weibull parameters at the three study sites.
findingOutcome: not suitable

findingStatement: GA and GM achieve the first- and second-best performance, respectively, when evaluated using MAE, RMSE, and R2.
findingScope: Catalca datasets for 2008–2010 at evaluated heights
findingOutcome: GA ranked first and GM ranked second.

findingStatement: EPF outperforms the other estimation methods when evaluated using NMAE and Chi-square error.
findingScope: Catalca datasets for 2008–2010 at evaluated heights
findingOutcome: EPF outperformed the other methods.

findingStatement: For the 2010 dataset, the Weibull PDF and CDF curves considerably deviate from the real-data curve, which the authors attribute to significant fluctuations in wind speeds.
findingOutcome: Considerable deviation from the real-data curve.

findingStatement: The site may not be suitable for year-round large-scale electricity generation under the current wind-turbine technique because of the cost factor.
findingOutcome: not suitable for year-round large-scale electricity generation under the stated conditions

findingStatement: For small-scale applications, the utilization of wind energy at the study site was still considered promising.
findingOutcome: promising for small-scale applications

findingStatement: Yearly average wind power densities of 74.00–122.48 W/m2 may be adequate for non-grid-connected electrical, mechanical, and agricultural applications.
findingOutcome: may be adequate for wind generators, battery charging, water pumping, and agricultural applications

findingStatement: With increasing hub height, the cost of energy reduces for all turbines.
findingScope: The four wind turbines assessed for Zahedan.
findingOutcome: Cost of energy decreases for all selected turbines.

findingStatement: If the wind-speed distribution is unimodal as at station A, superiority of the four mixture probability density functions and the maximum-entropy-principle probability density function relative to the conventional Weibull probability density function is not significant.
findingOutcome: not statistically significant superiority

findingStatement: When the distribution is bimodal as at stations B and C, all mixture probability density functions and the maximum-entropy-principle probability density function describe wind characterizations better than the Weibull probability density function, irrespective of wind-speed and power-density analyses.
findingScope: stations B and C; wind-speed and wind-power-density analyses
findingOutcome: describe wind characterizations better

findingStatement: For wind-speed analyses under bimodal distributions, the proposed Gamma–Weibull probability density function performs best in the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, followed by the Normal–Weibull and Weibull–Weibull probability density functions; the Normal–Normal probability density function performs worst except the Weibull probability density function.
findingScope: wind-speed analyses at stations B and C
findingOutcome: best Kolmogorov–Smirnov-test performance

findingStatement: Under bimodal distributions, no particular mixture probability density function or maximum-entropy-principle probability density function outperforms others in terms of RMSE or Chi-square error.
findingScope: RMSE and Chi-square-error analyses at stations B and C
findingOutcome: no particular model outperforms the others

findingStatement: For wind power density, the maximum-entropy-principle and Gamma–Weibull probability density functions describe best, followed by the Weibull–Weibull and Normal–Weibull probability density functions, especially in high speed ranges.
findingOutcome: best wind-power-density description

findingStatement: If POLARIS 62-1000 is operated at a hub height of 70 m and rated wind speed of 10 m/s, the capacity factors for Enugu, Owerri and Onitsha will be 59.17%, 8.20% and 16.99%, respectively.
findingOutcome: Projected capacity factors of 59.17%, 8.20% and 16.99% for Enugu, Owerri and Onitsha, respectively.

findingStatement: AEP has less variability as a function of the number of years because the sample standard deviation of AEP generally decreases according to the sample population.
findingScope: Expected annual energy production according to averaging periods and confidence intervals
findingOutcome: less variability in AEP

findingStatement: At Bechar, In Amenas and Ghardaia, about 55–75% of recorded wind speeds lie between cut-in speed of 3 m/s and rated speed of 13 m/s; a typical turbine with these specifications operates about 55–75% of the time at partial load.
findingOutcome: partial-load operation

findingStatement: At Adrar, only 12% of recorded wind speeds were less than 3 m/s; therefore, a wind turbine installed at this site can produce energy for about 88% of the time, with about 6% falling in the full-power range from 13 m/s to cut-out.
findingOutcome: wind turbine can produce energy for about 88% of the time

findingStatement: Under the assumed conditions in this study, the average LCOE for the P50-500 model in Minna showed to be the most economically viable option.
findingScope: Selected turbine models and locations considered in this study
findingOutcome: P50-500 model in Minna was the most economically viable option under the assumed conditions.

findingStatement: If a subsidy of about N6.00 or $0.0400 per kWh is provided by the government, the P50-500 model in Ilorin and Makurdi, and the P15-50 and P19-100 models in Minna, could also be economically worthwhile.
findingScope: Selected turbine models and locations considered in this study
findingOutcome: Additional turbine-location combinations could be economically worthwhile.

findingStatement: When the hub height is increased from 10 m to 30 m, the annual mean energy density increases by 79.57%.
findingOutcome: annual mean energy density increases by 79.57%

findingStatement: When the hub height is increased from 30 m to 50 m, the annual mean energy density increases by only 19.24%.
findingOutcome: annual mean energy density increases by only 19.24%

findingStatement: Bojnourd is a class 2 wind power site and Esfarayen, Nehbandan, and Fadashk are class 3 wind power sites, with consideration to wind power density classes published by the U.S. Department of Energy.
findingOutcome: The sites were indicated as suitable for both grid connection and stand-alone activities such as water pumping and battery charging.

findingStatement: At Katsina, cost of generating 1 kWh of electricity decreased with increasing hub height from 10 m until h = 50 m, where it was C0.0507 ≡ 111.25; further increase in hub height increased the modeled cost per kWh.
findingOutcome: least modeled cost per kWh and optimum hub height for favorable electricity generation

findingStatement: At a turbine hub height of h = 110 m at Katsina, simulated electric-power output Pe = 1714 W compared to the turbine rated power PeR = 1500 W.
findingOutcome: simulated electric-power output surpassed the rated power

findingStatement: With an increasing cut-in speed, the operation probability may drop identically at all concerned sites.
findingScope: Five concerned meteorological stations in Hong Kong.
findingOutcome: Operating probability decreases as cut-in speed increases.

findingStatement: The maximum percentage error between Weibull wind-speed frequencies and observed frequencies is 25% at wind speeds less than 2 m/s.
findingOutcome: maximum percentage error of 25%

findingStatement: At wind speeds greater than 2 m/s, the maximum variation between Weibull wind-speed frequencies and observed frequencies is about 5%, and the Weibull distribution fits the observed distribution reasonably well in the higher wind-speed range.
findingOutcome: about 5% maximum variation and reasonable fit at higher wind speeds

findingStatement: Season 3 (June to September) had a maximum overlap with the turbine power curve and consequently gave the maximum energy yield of 4571.55 kWh compared to the other seasons.
findingOutcome: maximum seasonal actual wind-energy yield

findingStatement: In the lower curtailment case of 0.8%, 120.6 MWh of yearly energy consumption can be met by WF1, equal to 18.16% of the average yearly energy consumption of pumps in the area.
findingOutcome: 120.6 MWh of demand met; 18.16% of average yearly pump energy consumption

findingStatement: In the 4.3% load-shedding case, 500.6 MWh of yearly energy consumption can be met by WF1, equal to 75.37% of the average yearly energy consumption of pumps in the area.
findingOutcome: 500.6 MWh of demand met; 75.37% of average yearly pump energy consumption

findingStatement: For lower load-shedding rates, WF4 with three wind turbines is the clear option, while for higher load-shedding rates of 4.3% the comparison is less clear and WF5 has a slightly better ratio.
findingScope: Comparison of CO2-emissions-to-demand-covered ratio among wind-farm scenarios
findingOutcome: WF4 is the clear option at lower load-shedding rates; WF5 has a slightly better ratio at 4.3%.

findingStatement: If wind speed distribution matches well with the Weibull function, EPFM, MOM and MSDM are applicable.
findingOutcome: EPFM, MOM and MSDM are applicable.

findingStatement: If wind speed distribution does not match well with the Weibull function, least-squares regression method can be considered based on cross checks including energy potential and cumulative distribution function.
findingOutcome: Least-squares regression method can be considered.

findingStatement: Based on the capacity-factor recommendation of more than 25%, each one of the seven turbines can be used for cost effective power generation in Dakhla and Laayoune.
findingScope: Dakhla and Laayoune; seven selected wind turbines
findingOutcome: cost effective power generation

findingStatement: Assila and Essouira were stated to be suitable only for stand-alone wind power applications, although their annual power densities of 180 W/m2 and 196 W/m2 fall within the 0–200 W/m2 interval categorized as "Not Suitable" in the paper's NREL classification table.
findingOutcome: conflicting_values

findingStatement: The wind speed and power densities of Kribi, Douala and Limbe are higher in the wet season than in the dry season and more wind power is expected to be harnessed in the wet season than in the dry season.
findingOutcome: Higher wind speed and power density in the wet season than in the dry season.

findingStatement: The four distributions did not fit observed wind speeds in August as accurately due to the high percentage of null winds.
findingScope: August observed wind speeds at Bohai Bay
findingOutcome: less accurate fitting

findingStatement: Higher wind speeds occurred during the dry season from November to July.
findingOutcome: higher wind speeds

findingStatement: Lower wind speeds occurred during the wet season from August to October.
findingOutcome: lower wind speeds

findingStatement: When using GWA to find good wind sites in north eastern Africa, the results are likely to be more reliable for less complex terrains like coastal regions.
findingOutcome: Global Wind Atlas results are likely to be more reliable.

findingStatement: The empirical methods of Justus and Lysen provided the highest performance when Weibull distribution was well fitted with observed wind speed data.
findingScope: Seven numerical methods evaluated in this study.
findingOutcome: highest performance

findingStatement: Maximum likelihood method gave better accuracy if Weibull distribution was not matched well to observed wind speed data. Otherwise, its accuracy was not desirable.
findingScope: Seven numerical methods evaluated in this study.
findingOutcome: better accuracy

findingStatement: Only EPFM, EMJ, EML, MOM, MLM and HM methods are recommended to estimate Weibull parameters to calculate average wind speeds with RPE lower than 10%.
findingOutcome: recommended methods

findingStatement: To calculate the monthly standard deviations and wind power densities on the site of Cotonou, it is preferable to use the Weibull parameters estimated by EPFM, EMJ, EML and MOM.
findingScope: Cotonou site; monthly standard deviations and monthly wind power densities
findingOutcome: preferable estimation methods

findingStatement: At low wind speed, the Weibull distributions, both probability and cumulative densities, fit rather poorly with the corresponding observed data; however, this inconvenience is tolerable because power production is extremely low at these wind speeds.
findingScope: Observed wind-speed data at İzmir–Aliağa, annual and winter comparison.
findingOutcome: Rather poor fit at low wind speeds, with the inconvenience described as tolerable because power production is extremely low.

findingStatement: The proposed Energy Variance Method provides the least error in case of Guwahati station.
findingOutcome: least error

findingStatement: The proposed Energy Variance Method provides the least error in case of Kolkata station.
findingOutcome: least error

findingStatement: The maximum likelihood method shows the least error in case of Shillong station.
findingOutcome: least error

findingStatement: The power density method shows the least error in case of Imphal station.
findingOutcome: least error

findingStatement: It is suggested to install small wind turbines instead of large wind turbines since average wind velocity is lower and ranges from 2.866 m/sec to 3.875 m/sec.
findingOutcome: Small wind turbines are suggested instead of large wind turbines.

findingStatement: The mixed-Weibull distribution is the most appropriate distribution even when the wind-speed data set does not show a bimodal distribution.
findingScope: Selected sites with unimodal or bimodal distributions and a very low percentage of null wind speeds.
findingOutcome: more appropriate distribution

findingStatement: At Athos, Kalamata and Santorini, p = 0, so the mixed-Weibull distribution is transformed to the typical simple-Weibull distribution; RMSE and R2 present the same values and both distributions give the same fitting to the experimental data.
findingOutcome: same fitting as the simple-Weibull distribution

findingStatement: Inverse Weibull distribution provides better fitting to wind-speed data measured in winter and autumn in Bursa.
findingOutcome: better fitting

findingStatement: Weibull distribution shows superior performance for modeling wind-speed data measured in spring and summer in Bursa.
findingOutcome: superior performance

findingStatement: Inverse Weibull distribution provides better fitting to model wind-speed data measured in Sakarya for all seasons.
findingOutcome: better fitting

findingStatement: Nak distribution function ranks 1st for Chabahar and Khaf stations with low skewness.
findingOutcome: highest performance

findingStatement: Nak distribution function shows lower effectiveness for the other stations with higher skewness.
findingOutcome: lower effectiveness

findingStatement: The greatest winds observed during the dry season correspond to months with the highest wind-turbine capacity factors, and the cost of electricity is lower during the dry season than during the rainy season.
findingScope: Around Kousseri and Maroua in the Far North Region.
findingOutcome: Higher capacity factors and lower cost of electricity during the dry season.

findingStatement: P-15-50 is the most interesting option for small communities or wind farms, with the highest capacity factor and the lowest cost of energy for its range of specific cost based on rated power.
findingOutcome: P-15-50 is the preferred option within its stated community-scale and specific-cost-range context.

findingStatement: TWD can provide better results than WD in terms of the power-error criterion for the considered wind-speed cases, except data which have a noticeably high positive skewness and kurtosis.
findingScope: considered wind-speed cases from the three Turkish stations
findingOutcome: TWD provides better power-error results except for data with noticeably high positive skewness and kurtosis.

findingStatement: The Weibull PDF seems to be better than the Burr PDF only episodically in the summer months.
findingOutcome: Weibull performed better than Burr only episodically.

findingStatement: Where wind components are close to Gaussian shape and without too much anisotropy, all fits are quite close and rather accurate, except on the tail where only the non-Gaussian distribution does not underestimate the strong-wind probability.
findingOutcome: does not underestimate strong-wind probability in the distribution tail

findingStatement: In complex mountain regions with anisotropy and/or departure from Gaussian wind-component shape, either the elliptical or the non-Gaussian distribution can be better suited than Weibull to represent wind statistics.
findingOutcome: can be better suited than Weibull

findingStatement: The Rayleigh–Rice distribution gives excellent results especially at weather stations in the Rhône or Aude valleys, where channelled flows create shouldered distributions that Weibull and other two-parameter distributions are not able to reproduce.
findingOutcome: gives excellent results and reproduces shouldered distributions

findingStatement: The Rayleigh–Rice distribution generally performs better during winter, which the authors explain by a higher probability of persistent strong winds producing a secondary peak or shoulder at higher wind speeds.
findingOutcome: generally performs better during winter

findingStatement: The mean wind-power expression for the Inverse Gamma distribution can only be used when parameter p is larger than 3; if p is less than 3, the reported mean value becomes negative because higher moments do not exist.
findingOutcome: The authors used a more general Monte Carlo integration approach for estimating mean wind power derived from the Inverse Gamma distribution.

findingStatement: Although the Weibull, GEV, and Nak distributions provided higher accuracy for lower wind speeds, the BS distribution gave better performance at higher wind-speed ranges that fall within the operational ranges of wind turbines.
findingOutcome: BS had better performance at higher wind-speed ranges within operational ranges of wind turbines.

findingStatement: The paper reports that the BS distribution gives the best fits at six stations, but reports conflicting ranks for the remaining four stations.
findingOutcome: conflicting_values

findingStatement: The agreement between model average-power estimates and empirical average-power estimates depends on how well models fit wind speeds between the cut-in and cut-out values of the power curve, and this predictive capability does not necessarily correspond to models' R2 values.
findingScope: Average wind turbine power output estimation using the Vestas V47-666 KW power curve.
findingOutcome: Kappa and Wakeby fit the upper-tail wind speeds that matter most for average turbine power output better than the bimodal Weibull in the illustrated comparisons.

findingStatement: For distributions presenting severe bimodal regimes, mixture distributions should be employed.
findingScope: All stations and heights considered in this study.
findingOutcome: Mixture distributions are required for adequate modeling of severe bimodal regimes.

findingStatement: For a station presenting a strong unimodal regime, like Al Mirfa, the fits given by the different models are all similar.
findingOutcome: Flexible models do not show a clear advantage under this strong unimodal regime.

findingStatement: At lower altitudes at the Masdar Wind Station, the more flexible model MWW/LS and KE clearly show an advantage while at 50 m, all models provide equivalent fits.
findingOutcome: Flexible models have an advantage at lower heights, whereas all models provide equivalent fits at 50 m.

findingStatement: No distribution was able to model the lower part of the particular histogram shape.
findingOutcome: Limitation of classical models in the presence of bimodality.

findingStatement: For stations with observed bimodal behavior, mixture distributions were necessary to adequately model the wind-speed distributions.
findingScope: About 5 of the 10 stations selected to illustrate the study results
findingOutcome: mixture distributions necessary for adequate modeling

findingStatement: The limited ability of the studied distributions to model wind speed at the Airport site is attributed to the bimodal shape of the histogram, with secondary maxima in medium intensity wind speeds.

For the elevated sites and regarding the fit of the probability distributions for the overall period, the Gamma distribution fit is systematically superior compared to Weibull, partly due to its ability to model more efficiently the medium and tail of the distribution.
findingScope: Elevated Malaxa, Airport, and especially Pedio Volis sites; overall period
findingOutcome: Gamma distribution fit is systematically superior to Weibull.

findingStatement: No conventional parametric distribution can properly match the bimodal histograms because all conventional parametric distributions considered are unimodal distributions with only one single peak, whereas the non-parametric kernel estimation could fit well the bimodal probability density distributions.
findingScope: Qingdao and Dalian wind-speed histograms in this study.
findingOutcome: The kernel density model fit bimodal probability-density distributions better than the conventional parametric distributions considered.

findingStatement: For Gisenyi, the conclusion reports Gamma (p=3.44; β=0.85), followed by lognormal (μ=1.27; σ=0.50) and Weibull (k=1.99; c=4.58), as the more suitable distribution functions.
findingOutcome: Reported distribution ranking

findingStatement: For Gisenyi, Section 3.2 states that the lognormal distribution corresponds to the best fit of the data set, followed by the Gamma distribution and the Weibull distribution.
findingOutcome: Reported distribution ranking

findingStatement: For Kigali, the conclusion reports Gamma (p=13.29; β=4.64), followed by normal (μ=2.86; σ=0.78) and lognormal (μ=1.02; σ=0.26), as the more suitable distribution functions.
findingOutcome: Reported distribution ranking

findingStatement: For Kigali, Section 3.2 states that the lognormal distribution corresponds to the best fit of the data set, followed by the Gamma distribution and normal distribution.
findingOutcome: Reported distribution ranking

findingStatement: For Butare, Weibull (k=4.93; c=2.86) corresponds to the best fit of the data set, followed by normal (μ=2.62; σ=0.64) and Gamma (p=16.60; β=6.33).
findingOutcome: Reported distribution ranking

findingStatement: For Kamembe, the conclusion reports Gamma (p=2.99; β=1.33), followed by lognormal (μ=0.66; σ=0.54) and Weibull (k=2.38; c=2.74), as the more suitable distribution functions.
findingOutcome: Reported distribution ranking

findingStatement: For Kamembe, Section 3.2 states that Gamma (p=2.99; β=1.33) corresponds to the best fit of the data set, followed by Weibull (k=2.38; c=2.74) and lognormal (μ=0.66; σ=0.54).
findingOutcome: Reported distribution ranking

findingStatement: When wind speed data regimes present skewed bimodality and kurtotic unimodality, non-mixture distributions cannot explain the whole regime at these stations.
findingScope: UAE meteorological stations with skewed bimodality and kurtotic unimodality
findingOutcome: Non-mixture distributions provide an insufficient fit under these distributional characteristics.

findingStatement: For wind speed data with skewed unimodality, the improvement resulting from the application of mixture distributions is less important than the improvement obtained for skewed bimodality and kurtotic unimodality.
findingScope: Al Mirfa and Al Wagan stations
findingOutcome: The improvement from mixture distributions is less important.

findingStatement: For Al Mirfa and Al Wagan stations, non-mixture distributions can compete with mixture distributions in modeling wind speed data.
findingScope: Al Mirfa and Al Wagan stations
findingOutcome: Non-mixture distributions can compete with mixture distributions.

findingStatement: For Pylos and Mar de Alboran, wind power density takes its maximum value for the prevailing wind direction.
findingOutcome: Maximum wind power density occurred at the prevailing wind direction.

findingStatement: For Andros, the maximum of the wind power density curve is obtained for the mean wind direction, suggesting that the most probable value of wind direction is not necessarily the one that provides the maximum wind power density.
findingOutcome: The mean wind direction, rather than necessarily the most probable wind direction, provided the maximum wind power density.

findingStatement: When the criterion for the best fit is formulated in terms of wind-energy characteristics such as mean wind power density or average wind turbine power output, the results were quite different: the best-fit distribution with respect to wind speed is not necessarily the best-fit solution with respect to wind-energy characteristics.
findingOutcome: Wind-speed-fit and wind-energy-characteristic-fit evaluations are not equivalent tasks.

findingStatement: For the average wind turbine power output in Greek waters, all obtained relative errors for JSB were systematically smaller than 6.34% for all locations.
findingOutcome: RelativePercentError smaller than 6.34%

findingStatement: For the average wind turbine power output in Spanish waters, JSB, KAP and WEI were the only distributions with a consistently very good behavior, since all obtained relative errors were smaller than 7.6% for all locations.
findingOutcome: RelativePercentError smaller than 7.6%

findingStatement: Highest and lowest modeled annual wind energy yield occurs in highly textured terrain within very small distances (<500 m).
findingOutcome: Strong local spatial variation in modeled annual wind energy yield.

findingStatement: Modeled wind-speed values are predominantly higher at sites exposed to the West and Southwest.
findingOutcome: Higher modeled wind speeds.

findingStatement: The CPSO–Weibull model was best for study site C, while the CS–Weibull model was best for the other three sites, based on maximum R2.
findingOutcome: CPSO–Weibull was selected at site C; CS–Weibull was selected at sites A, B and D.

findingStatement: CS–GEV performed best in all cases except for quarterly offshore extreme wind speeds in site D, where CPSO–GEV performed better when PE was selected as the major criterion.
findingScope: monthly and quarterly offshore extreme wind-speed fitting at four study sites
findingOutcome: CPSO–GEV was selected for quarterly extreme wind speeds at site D.

findingStatement: For site A during Oct.–Dec., PSO elicited the best outcomes when GWO did not elicit the best results.
findingOutcome: PSO was best for this reported period.

findingStatement: For site C during Jul.–Sep., CS was the best method when GWO was the worst.
findingOutcome: CS was best for this reported period.

findingStatement: When estimating W1 and MTNW, DKDM is the obvious winner with respect to methods that do not consider boundary correction.
findingScope: Simulated parametric distribution models W1 and MTNW.
findingOutcome: better performance near the zero boundary

findingStatement: In the regions away from zero, densities estimated by DKDM and SJPI nearly coincide; near zero, DKDM has a non-negative density domain while SJPI extends to the negative axle.
findingScope: Probability-density estimates for wind-speed data from the six observation stations.
findingOutcome: DKDM avoids negative wind-speed density-domain estimates near zero.

findingStatement: The farm power generation estimated using the MMWD model is 5% lower than that estimated using the Weibull distribution, although the WPD given by MMWD is higher.
findingScope: Nine-turbine wind farm at the Baker site based on ten-year wind data.
findingOutcome: Lower estimated farm power generation despite higher estimated WPD.

findingStatement: MEP-derived distributions outperform conventional statistical distributions for the wind-speed data from Benedict.
findingOutcome: outperform

findingStatement: For data from the other sites, one or more conventional distributions can always be found that outperform MEP-derived distributions.
findingScope: Alfred, Green River, Olga, and Ray/Wheelock
findingOutcome: outperformed by one or more conventional distributions

findingStatement: Mixture probability density functions are clearly superior to all one-component probability density functions according to the four probability-probability-plot goodness-of-fit metrics.
findingOutcome: superior fit

findingStatement: The Wakeby probability density function is often an appropriate choice for modeling the upper tail of empirical wind-speed probability density functions.
findingOutcome: appropriate upper-tail fit

findingStatement: The Kappa probability density function was appropriate for estimating the upper tail of many offshore empirical wind-speed probability density functions.
findingOutcome: appropriate upper-tail fit

findingStatement: Generalized Extreme Value-Weibull is able to accurately reproduce both modes of the empirical wind-speed probability density function.
findingScope: Venezuela grid cell at latitude 8°N and longitude 67°W
findingOutcome: accurately reproduces both modes

findingStatement: The widely used two-parameter Weibull probability density function provided similarly good fits only in a few cases.
findingScope: Global onshore and offshore wind-speed regimes evaluated in this study
findingOutcome: similarly good fit only in a few cases

findingStatement: The results of this study may change for sites with high wind potential.
findingOutcome: Results may change.

findingStatement: The lognormal distribution function yields the best fit to the wind data.
findingScope: Five studied stations in Kerman Province
findingOutcome: best fit

findingStatement: For truncated wind-speed data, Weibull distribution with MLE parameter estimation did best to fit the wind-speed distribution for Bam, Arzuiyeh, and Shahrbabak.
findingOutcome: better fit

findingStatement: The Rayleigh distribution gave the least accurate results compared to both actual and truncated wind data.
findingOutcome: least accurate results

findingStatement: The GL distribution has the lowest RMSE and AIC and the highest R2 and lnL values.
findingScope: Winter wind-speed data at all stations.
findingOutcome: better fitting

findingStatement: The Weibull distribution has the lowest RMSE and AIC values and the highest R2 and lnL values.
findingOutcome: best model

findingStatement: The GL distribution is most preferable in terms of lnL and AIC, whereas Weibull provides the best model when RMSE and R2 criteria are considered.
findingOutcome: model ranking depends on the evaluation criterion

findingStatement: Weibull and PL distributions are more preferable than the GL distribution in most cases; however, GL has substantial improvement over PL and Weibull for Bilecik in winter and Sakarya in summer.
findingScope: Annual and seasonal wind-speed data at Bilecik, Bursa, Eskisehir, and Sakarya.
findingOutcome: PDE-based performance differs from fitting-criterion performance

findingStatement: Among the ten sites considered, site WM05 had the highest capacity factor for all turbines.
findingScope: WM01 to WM10 and the 20 turbines considered
findingOutcome: highest capacity factor

findingStatement: Among the ten sites considered, site WM02 had the lowest capacity factor.
findingScope: WM01 to WM10 and the 20 turbines considered
findingOutcome: lowest capacity factor

findingOutcome: higher capacity factor

findingStatement: More wind power can be harnessed during the day compared to the night, with most turbines except at site WM07, which had a higher turbine capacity factor during the night.

findingStatement: The evening electricity peak periods (18:00–20:00) had a higher capacity factor than the morning peak periods (07:00–10:00) at all sites.
findingOutcome: higher capacity factor than morning peak periods

findingStatement: For the uni-modal illustrations, Weibull, Rayleigh and Gaussian distributions show approximately similar R2 values varying from 0.95 to 0.99, although the R2 value is closer to 1.0 for the Gaussian fit probability distribution.

findingStatement: For the bi-modal illustrations, the R2 value is close to 1 in the case of the Gaussian function and much lower for Weibull and Rayleigh distribution functions.
findingOutcome: Gaussian fit outperforms Weibull and Rayleigh fit by R2.

findingStatement: For bi-modal and multi-modal curve fitting, the R2 value is significantly higher for Gaussian fit when compared with Weibull and Rayleigh distribution functions.
findingScope: Multi-modal illustrations and the reported 208-site exercise
findingOutcome: Gaussian fit has significantly higher R2.

findingStatement: For the Mitsubishi Galant, up to 37% of the energy could be recovered on the Edinburgh route, but this figure decreased to 23% when the calculation was carried out on flat terrain.
findingOutcome: Energy recovery decreased to 23% under the flat-terrain calculation.

findingStatement: Wind potential is suitable for wind-turbine applications using taller wind towers.
findingScope: hilltops and exposed ridge tops surrounding Maroua
findingOutcome: suitable

findingStatement: Wind potential is most suitable for wind-turbine applications.
findingScope: hilltops and exposed ridge tops surrounding Maroua
findingOutcome: most suitable

findingStatement: Wind potential is excellent for wind-turbine applications.
